slides.text: In 1968, five machines hung from a gallery ceiling in London and tried to court each other with light.
The British scientist Gordon Pask built them for Cybernetic Serendipity, a show of art made with computers and machines.
Two of them were “male.” Each sent out a flashing beam of light, looking for a partner.
Three were “female.” They carried mirrors that could catch a beam and send it back.
A female answered with a sound. If her mirror returned his light to the right spot, the male was satisfied.
The females had to learn where to aim their mirrors.
Visitors could walk in among them and interrupt.
Fifty years later, in 2018, a design school in Detroit rebuilt all five from the historical record.
Today all five belong to ZKM, a museum of art and media in Karlsruhe, in Germany.
